case_study_insert.main_stem: Nestwood Eco Boards (NEB) is a private limited company in the eco-friendly building board sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2015 by Priya Nestor, it makes straw-fibre boards for green construction projects and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. NEB plans to invest $720,000 in a new board-pressing line using low-formaldehyde eco-resin, financed by a $300,000 bank loan, a $250,000 share issue and $170,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $286,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. NEB faces two problems: waste on the old board line is 3.8%, and 12 of its operators are not yet certified on the new press.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary, 2025: a survey of 350 architects and builders' merchants found that 62% prefer low-formaldehyde eco boards and 54% would pay up to $0.60 more per board. Defect complaints on standard board fell from 26 to 14 per 1,000 boards. Delivery lead time averages 6 days. A quality log records waste of 3.8% on the old line against 1.9% on the new pilot line. Training records show 12 of 48 operators trained on the new press; certification courses cost $680 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Nestwood Eco Boards for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate rose from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing loan and overdraft costs for borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage increased 6.2% from $12.90 to $13.70 an hour from April 2026. (3) Straw and resin input prices rose 8.4% year-on-year while construction inflation reached 5.5% and green-building sales grew 4.1%.

questions.question_text: NEB financed $170,000 of its $720,000 expansion with retained profit. Explain two advantages for NEB of using retained profit rather than a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment schedule, which eases NEB's cash flow while it carries fixed costs of $286,000 a year and a $300,000 bank loan. The $170,000 can be deployed immediately to install the low-formaldehyde eco-resin press without lender approval, helping NEB cut waste from 3.8% toward the 1.9% achieved on the pilot line.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps Priya Nestor's control intact and avoids pledging assets as collateral, so the $720,000 board-pressing line is not at risk of repossession if green-building demand disappoints. It also preserves the $250,000 share issue and existing cash for working capital, giving NEB room to wait the average 6-day delivery cycle and to meet its share of the 8.4% rise in resin costs without returning to the bank.

Keeping the $170,000 internal also preserves headroom under the $286,000 fixed-cost base while the 12 uncertified operators are trained and waste moves from 3.8% toward the 1.9% pilot rate.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NEB's retained profit, loan and waste data.

questions.question_text: NEB is launching its low-formaldehyde eco boards. Consider trade journals and builders' merchant exhibitions, social media campaigns, or sponsorship of a green-building award. Which should NEB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade journals and merchants' exhibitions: These reach the 350 architects and builders' merchants in NEB's own survey directly, where 62% prefer low-formaldehyde eco boards and 54% would pay $0.60 more. Technical stands let NEB show the 1.9% pilot waste figure and certification evidence, and generate specification decisions and orders quickly. The drawbacks are stand costs and a narrow audience, but for a 48-employee firm funding a $720,000 line the targeting is efficient.

Social media campaigns: Social platforms can build broad awareness of green construction cheaply and can be measured, with creative content showing the straw-fibre production story. However, most users are householders rather than the architects and merchants who specify boards, so engagement may not convert into the volume needed to fill 72,000 units of capacity, and the 6-day delivery cycle limits any direct-sales benefit.

Green-building award sponsorship: Sponsorship would raise NEB's profile among sustainability-minded developers and could support a premium brand, fitting the 54% premium signal. It is, however, the most expensive and least controllable of the three, with no guaranteed orders, and its impact is slow compared with the immediate specification conversations available at trade events.

Recommendation: NEB should choose trade journals and merchants' exhibitions. They reach the exact 350 surveyed specifiers, convert the 62% preference and 54% premium into orders, and cost far less than sponsorship, which is rejected as indirect and expensive. Social media is rejected as too consumer-focused to fill the $720,000 line; NEB can use it later as cheap supporting awareness.

Even with slower build-up than television, the 6-day delivery cycle rewards the direct orders exhibitions generate rather than broad awareness alone, which suits a firm with $286,000 of annual fixed costs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with little NEB context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to NEB's surveyed specifiers.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why social media and sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: NEB uses a flat structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for NEB of this approach in tackling the 3.8% waste on its board line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure shortens the chain of command between the workforce of 48 and Priya Nestor, so operators can report the causes of the 3.8% waste immediately and managers can respond without layers of approval. Faster feedback helped the pilot line reach 1.9% waste, and the same quick communication is essential when a press setting drifts and scraps a batch of low-formaldehyde boards.

Point 2: Democratic leadership invites the 12 trained operators and other staff to suggest improvements to the pressing process, raising ownership and motivation. Workers who help design waste-reduction routines are more likely to follow them, which supports NEB's aim of matching the 1.9% pilot rate and protects the $14.00 selling price and $7.50 variable cost from being undermined by scrap. Higher involvement can also ease the gap where 12 of 48 staff still need certification.

Shorter communication lines also make it easier to share the 1.9% pilot practice across all 48 staff, so waste reduction does not depend on a handful of trained operators.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NEB's waste, structure and staff.

questions.question_text: NEB must train 12 of its 48 operators on the new press. Consider on-the-job training or external certification courses at $680 per person. Which should NEB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning beside the new press is directly relevant to NEB's own low-formaldehyde process and costs no course fees, and the 12 operators stay productive while learning, which protects output of 72,000 units. Trainers know the exact settings that delivered 1.9% waste on the pilot, so improvements can be passed on immediately. The downside is that no recognised certificate is issued, and 54% of surveyed buyers pay a premium for certified eco boards, so NEB may struggle to prove competence to merchants; experienced operators also lose time from coaching.

External certification: Courses at $680 for each of the 12 staff cost 12 × $680 = $8,160, affordable against the $720,000 investment, and give a formal credential that supports the 62% preference for low-formaldehyde eco boards. They also bring in outside expertise that could cut the 3.8% waste faster. However, sending 12 of 48 operators off site reduces pressing capacity, and a generic course may not cover NEB's specific resin and press settings, so follow-up on site would still be needed.

Decision: NEB should choose on-the-job training as the main method. It is cheaper, machine-specific, keeps the 12 staff producing, and directly transfers the pilot line's 1.9% waste practice into full production. External courses are rejected as the primary route because the $8,160 and the lost press time are unnecessary when NEB's own operators already hold the relevant know-how; NEB should add short external certification later if merchants demand formal proof.

With the $8,160 saved, NEB can fund refresher sessions later, so the decision keeps cash available while the $286,000 fixed costs and the $300,000 loan are being serviced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with little NEB application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to NEB's 12 staff and waste target.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the $8,160 computation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NEB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $286,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $7.50) = $286,000 ÷ $6.50 = 44,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 44,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $7.50 = $6.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NEB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 44,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 72,000 units to show a margin of safety of 28,000 units, indicating how far green-building orders could fall before the new line stops covering costs.
2. Use the $6.50 contribution per unit to judge the $0.60 premium: accepting it lifts contribution to $7.10, so managers can decide whether to offer merchants a smaller discount and still cover the $286,000 fixed costs.
3. Check that output can service the $300,000 bank loan and the $250,000 share issue: at 72,000 units NEB is well above break-even, so managers can stress-test a drop in orders.
4. Track unit cost of $11.47 ($286,000 ÷ 72,000 units + $7.50) each quarter; a rising figure would flag that the 3.8% waste is returning and prompt corrective action.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 44,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 28,000-unit margin of safety vs 72,000 output; $0.60 premium modelling against $286,000 fixed costs; servicing the $300,000 loan and $250,000 share issue; and $11.47 unit-cost benchmarking to track 3.8% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NEB's profitability. Has NEB's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $900,000 to $1,050,000 while cost of sales moved from $540,000 to $588,000, lifting gross profit from $360,000 to $462,000. Operating profit grew from $108,000 to $189,000 and capital employed from $900,000 to $1,050,000, while interest payable rose from $9,000 to $14,000.

Evaluation: Every measure improved. Gross margin moved from 40.0% to 44.0%, showing better control of straw and resin costs as the new press reduces waste from 3.8% toward 1.9%. Operating margin jumped from 12.0% to 18.0% because operating profit grew far faster than revenue, evidence of fixed-cost leverage as output approaches 72,000 units. Returns on capital rose from 12.0% to 18.0%, so the $720,000 pressing line is generating more profit per dollar employed despite the new loan and share issue. The caution is that NEB is small and its 6-day delivery cycle and 8.4% input inflation could squeeze these margins if green-building sales slow from 4.1%.

Conclusion: NEB's profitability has improved decisively: gross margin, operating margin and ROCE all rose together. The investment is already adding returns, so the priority is to protect the 44.0% gross margin by locking in straw and resin supply and converting the 54% premium interest into actual orders.

Operating profit grew far faster than revenue, so the gain reflects leverage over fixed costs rather than one favourable contract; even allowing for the rise in interest payable to $14,000, the trend is clearly upward.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates margins and returns for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NEB of using low-formaldehyde eco-resin in its straw-fibre eco boards.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Low-formaldehyde resin supports the green positioning that 62% of the 350 surveyed architects prefer and the 54% who would pay $0.60 more, helping NEB protect its $6.50 contribution per unit and differentiate while straw and resin input prices rise 8.4%. The pilot line's 1.9% waste, against 3.8% on the old line, suggests the new process also cuts scrap cost.

Disadvantage: Eco-resin typically costs more than standard adhesive, which would lift the $7.50 variable cost per unit and require the full $0.60 premium to be realised across all 72,000 boards to avoid margin loss. If merchants resist, NEB must either accept a lower contribution or push the $14.00 price above what buyers will pay, risking the 54% premium signal.

NEB must pass the premium on consistently to the 350 surveyed specifiers, since the $286,000 fixed costs leave little room if the 54% premium interest is not converted into actual board orders.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using NEB's survey, costs and pilot data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 8.4% rise in straw and resin input costs will affect NEB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If NEB's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage points cost 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). This is modest against fixed costs of $286,000 and can be removed by fixing the rate; the main secondary risk is that dearer credit discourages the green-building customers whose sales grew 4.1%.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.70 an hour): With a workforce of 48, some production and packing hours are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours or individual pay, so any annual wage total would be invented; the sound comparison is productivity of 72,000 units ÷ 48 staff = 1,500 units per worker. If that holds, the rise is absorbable; if output slips, unit labour cost climbs and the $6.50 contribution per unit falls.

Straw and resin input costs (8.4%): These feeds directly into board production. Since the $7.50 variable cost is not broken down, only a labelled bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 8.4%, that is 8.4% × $7.50 = $0.63 a unit, and across 72,000 boards about $45,360 a year (72,000 × $0.63). Even a partial pass-through erodes the $6.50 contribution that must cover $286,000 fixed costs and service the $720,000 expansion, though the $0.60 eco premium offers some recovery.

Conclusion: The 8.4% rise in straw and resin costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every board, directly attacks the contribution that underpins the investment, and cannot be neutralised by fixing a loan rate. The interest effect is small and controllable, and the wage rise can be offset while 1,500-units-per-worker productivity holds, so both are smaller threats.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited NEB application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NEB's costs or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
